definition: the state of being everywhere at once
memoryTip: Ubi (Latin “where”) + everywhere — so common it’s hard to escape.
correctPassage: The ubiquity of smartphones has reshaped how students research and study.
wrongPassages: The mountain’s ubiquity made it a rare landmark only locals could find.
After the store closed, the product’s ubiquity left empty shelves worldwide.
She prized the painting’s ubiquity, since no other copy existed.

definition: not harmful or offensive; harmless
memoryTip: In- (not) + noxious (harmful) — a remark that doesn’t sting.
correctPassage: What seemed an innocuous joke later made several coworkers uncomfortable.
wrongPassages: The innocuous chemical burned through the steel drum within minutes.
Police evacuated the block after detecting an innocuous gas leak.
Critics called the speech innocuous after it sparked protests in three cities.

definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow
memoryTip: Think of a volume coiled into tight twists — overly complex.
correctPassage: The contract’s convoluted clauses left neither side sure who held liability.
wrongPassages: Her convoluted explanation used one clear sentence anyone could follow.
The map was convoluted: a single straight highway with no turns.
He gave a convoluted answer that cut straight to the main point.

definition: most noticeable or important; standing out
memoryTip: From Latin salire, “to leap” — points that leap out at you.
correctPassage: The most salient finding was the sharp drop in error rates after training.
wrongPassages: The report buried its salient details where no one would notice them.
She called the typo salient and ignored the main experimental result.
His salient role meant he barely appeared in the project at all.

definition: to prevent someone from accomplishing something
memoryTip: A thwart is a cross-seat in a boat — something that blocks your path.
correctPassage: Bad weather threatened to thwart the launch for a third time.
wrongPassages: The coach’s pep talk helped thwart the team toward an easy win.
New funding will thwart the lab’s long-delayed experiment at last.
Security cameras were installed to thwart customers and make shopping smoother.

definition: to delay or block by creating an obstacle
memoryTip: Im-pede: put something in the path of the feet — slow progress.
correctPassage: Debris on the track will impede the train’s progress until crews clear it.
wrongPassages: Extra tutors will impede struggling students toward higher scores.
The new express lane will impede rush-hour traffic so cars move faster.
Fresh supplies impede recovery by giving the hospital what it needs.

definition: to gather information bit by bit from various sources
memoryTip: Farmers glean leftover grain — pick up scraps of info the same way.
correctPassage: From scattered letters, historians can glean how the town responded to the crisis.
wrongPassages: She chose to glean the entire archive in one uninterrupted reading.
Investigators gleaned the truth by inventing details no source had provided.
He would glean every document into the shredder before anyone could read it.

definition: lasting only a very short time
memoryTip: Ephemera once meant “for a day” — here today, gone tomorrow.
correctPassage: Social media fame is often ephemeral, fading within a few weeks.
wrongPassages: Stone monuments are ephemeral because they outlast the people who built them.
Their ephemeral friendship has continued through thirty years of weekly letters.
He locked the ephemeral records in a vault marked permanent archive.

definition: occasionally; at irregular intervals
memoryTip: In scattered spots — now and then, not on a steady schedule.
correctPassage: The rare bird appears only sporadically along this stretch of coast.
wrongPassages: The factory whistle blew sporadically at the same minute every morning.
She practiced sporadically: two hours every day without missing a session.
Trains arrived sporadically on a published timetable that never changed.

definition: filled with something undesirable; tense with risk
memoryTip: Freighted with trouble — loaded down with tension or danger.
correctPassage: The negotiations were fraught with misunderstandings from the first meeting.
wrongPassages: Their vacation was fraught with calm beaches and uninterrupted sleep.
The simple recipe was fraught with only three ingredients and one pan.
He found the empty hallway fraught with silence and no conflict at all.

definition: in a way that suggests a favorable outcome
memoryTip: Auspicious omens once came from watching birds — a promising start.
correctPassage: The festival began auspiciously with clear skies and a packed opening night.
wrongPassages: The merger opened auspiciously when both CEOs resigned on day one.
Rain flooded the field, so the season started auspiciously for outdoor sports.
She took the rejection letter as an auspiciously clear sign to quit altogether.

definition: in a random, unplanned, or careless way
memoryTip: Hap (chance) + hazard — by luck, not by plan; messy.
correctPassage: Files had been stored haphazardly, with no consistent naming system.
wrongPassages: The engineer arranged every cable haphazardly according to a detailed blueprint.
She packed haphazardly, labeling each box and checking items off a list.
They marched haphazardly in perfect formation down the parade route.

definition: showing opposition or hostility
memoryTip: Like a story’s antagonist — opposing, not cooperative.
correctPassage: The two theories are not necessarily antagonistic; they address different scales.
wrongPassages: Her antagonistic tone put everyone at ease within the first minute.
The partners signed an antagonistic agreement to share profits equally.
Neighbors held an antagonistic block party to welcome new families.

definition: a summary; the act of adding things up
memoryTip: Sum it up — a total or a closing overview.
correctPassage: The final chapter is a careful summation of the book’s main claims.
wrongPassages: Her summation skipped any overview and opened with brand-new evidence.
He offered a summation that listed every footnote and never closed the argument.
The lawyer’s summation was a raw first draft she had not yet organized.

definition: leaving no doubt; clear and unambiguous
memoryTip: Un-equi-vocal: not two voices — one clear meaning only.
correctPassage: The data provide unequivocal support for the revised timeline.
wrongPassages: His unequivocal answer was “maybe, depending on several unknowns.”
The map was unequivocal: three conflicting routes and no legend.
She gave an unequivocal shrug that left the committee more confused than before.

definition: beyond criticism; faultless
memoryTip: You can’t reproach (blame) them — conduct with no fault to find.
correctPassage: Her professional conduct throughout the inquiry was irreproachable.
wrongPassages: The audit found his irreproachable books riddled with missing receipts.
Critics praised the film as irreproachable for its endless plot holes.
An irreproachable alibi collapsed when security video showed him at the scene.

definition: relating to mental links or connections between ideas
memoryTip: Works by association — memory links, not strict step-by-step logic.
correctPassage: The poem relies on associative leaps rather than a linear plot.
wrongPassages: His associative essay never linked one image or idea to another.
The sealed cube was redesigned to be associative: no doors between rooms.
She preferred associative notes that listed facts in isolation with no connections.

definition: impossible to avoid or resist
memoryTip: In-e-luctable: you can’t struggle free — the outcome is locked in.
correctPassage: Climate models point to ineluctable warming under current emissions paths.
wrongPassages: He called the puzzle ineluctable after solving it in under a minute.
Voters tabled the ineluctable transit tax that most riders already supported.
The coach treated the loss as ineluctable, then changed strategy and won the rematch.

definition: very weak, thin, or slight
memoryTip: Thin as a tenuous thread — a weak link that may snap.
correctPassage: The link between the two studies remains tenuous at best.
wrongPassages: Their tenuous alliance has held firm through three decades of crisis.
She built a tenuous case packed with undisputed documents and witnesses.
The bridge’s tenuous steel beams made engineers confident it would last a century.

definition: to fail by trying to do or control too much
memoryTip: Reach too far — stretch beyond your power and fall short.
correctPassage: Critics accused the agency of regulatory overreach into local decisions.
wrongPassages: The careful plan showed overreach by staying well within the budget.
Her modest goals were praised as overreach by colleagues who wanted more ambition.
With limited staff, their overreach kept projects small and fully finished.
